paragraphs: §1 — The book of "our colleague"; the Torah's recondite meanings; prophets and priests as its expositors

[Lead-in, from the close of Bab 6:] … and he informed that all creation comes to pray before Him in the Sanctuary at the new moons and on the days of the Sabbaths. And he also informed, in this account, of the censure of the eaters of swine's flesh and of the rest of the forbidden things, and informed that they perish and are cut off — that being in his saying [Isa 66:17] אֹכְלֵי בְּשַׂר הַחֲזִיר וְהַשֶּׁקֶץ וְהָעַכְבָּר יַחְדָּו יָסֻפוּ נְאֻם יְיָ ("the eaters of swine's flesh and the vermin and the mouse shall together come to an end, says the Lord") — while you claim that all the beasts, swine and otherwise, were released and their eating made lawful by the coming of Jesus. So would one in whom there is the least sense advance such a statement, let alone one who lays claim to knowledge and inquiry? And since we said that a people of those who profess our religion have shared with them in the statement that the temple promised to be built has [already] passed and elapsed, and likewise all the good tidings — we shall, after this, also examine that which corrupts the statement of all [of them]. And we wish now to mention and make plain what we promised, of mentioning what is in Scripture that necessitates the eternal reward and punishment (al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb al-abadī) which the Christians spoke of and claimed has no trace in Scripture.
Bab 7. On establishing reward and punishment from the Torah and the rest of the books of the prophets.

One of our colleagues (baʿḍ aṣḥābinā) composed a book on this subject, in which he drew out the discussion at some length; so we abridge his discussion of it, and add to it also some of what he overlooked and did not mention. He said: Our book [the Torah] is a book of exalted meanings, recondite [in them], wide of seas; and within it there are sciences that none attains save one who is set apart and pre-eminent in the science of sound analogy (ʿilm al-qiyās al-ṣaḥīḥ) and in the rational sciences (al-ʿulūm al-ʿaqliyya). For this reason [David] says [Ps 119:18] גַּל עֵינַי וְאַבִּיטָה נִפְלָאוֹת מִתּוֹרָתֶךָ ("uncover my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of Your Torah") etc. For had this excellent sage not known that within this book are wonders that need to be apprehended, he would not have besought his Lord to disclose that to him.

And the prophets (peace be upon them) after Moses — his mention be for good — used to uncover thing after thing of what was recondite of the meanings of this book, I mean the Torah. And likewise the imams who were the sons of Aaron (peace be upon him), who were attached to the Sanctuary for the offering of the sacrifices — they too used to uncover, of the recondite of its meanings, things of the kind that the prophets used to uncover; and they sometimes stood in the station of the prophets in informing of the unseen — that being by means of the אֵפוֹד and the אוּרִים וְתֻמִּים. For this reason Scripture said [Mal 2:7] כִּי שִׂפְתֵי כֹהֵן יִשְׁמְרוּ דַעַת ("for the lips of the priest guard knowledge") etc. So when the house of Israel were exiled and scattered, and the two parties — I mean the prophets and the priests together — were lost, they were dispersed and fell into disagreement over the doctrines and the beliefs. And were it not for the kindness of the Maker (majestic and mighty) to us by [granting us] the books of those who came after Moses among the prophets, who expounded part of what he said and interpreted it, our state in the matter of ignorance would have been the worst of states. For if the books of the philosophers — who are not prophets, and whose speech is not the speech of the Creator (majestic and holy) — have needed interpreters to interpret their meanings, such as Alexander of Aphrodisias (al-Iskandar al-Afrūdīsī), and Porphyry (Furfūriyūs), and the like of [the grammarian] al-Naḥwī …

: The bab opens by naming, but not identifying, its principal source: "one of our colleagues" (baʿḍ aṣḥābinā) who wrote a treatise on otherworldly reward and punishment, which Q here abridges (nakhtaṣiru kalāmahu) and supplements (nuḍīfu ilayhi … baʿḍ mā aghfala). The phrase aṣḥābunā is Q's standard designation for fellow Karaites; the predecessor is unidentified, but the eschatology that follows — the survival of the soul, the two-stage resurrection (body-and-soul in the Garden, then disembodied angelic souls in al-dahr), and the "life/death = reward/punishment" lexical thesis — is the kind of developed doctrine associated with the early Karaite mutakallimūn. Q's interpolations are flagged through the bab by the shift from "he said" (qāla) to "we say" (naqūlu / naḥtāju). : The sentence trails off at the page foot; the apodosis ("… how much more does the Torah need its prophetic interpreters") is supplied by the sense and resumed in §2. The a fortiori is pointed: pagan philosophical texts required commentators — Alexander of Aphrodisias and Porphyry being the canonical late-antique exegetes of Aristotle, mediated to Q through the Baghdad-Christian Aristotelian school (Mattā b. Yūnus, Yaḥyā b. ʿAdī) — so the divinely-revealed Torah, a fortiori, needs its prophetic expositors. "al-Naḥwī" ("the grammarian") is left as Q gives it; it most plausibly designates John Philoponus (Yaḥyā al-Naḥwī), the standard Arabic sobriquet, completing the trio of late-antique Greek commentators. The remark that the loss of prophets and priests at the Exile produced doctrinal ikhtilāf (sectarian disagreement) is a Karaite topos: the post-prophetic confusion is what made authoritative interpretation necessary.
§2 — The legislative analogy: Scripture states the limit-case and leaves the rest to qiyās

… the [law of the] idol: every idol upon which [the case] must be measured by analogy (yuqās ʿalayhi) — for stoning and killing were obligatory only upon him who set his offspring to this [Molech-worship] alone. The like of that is His saying in Exodus [Exod 21:33] וְכִי יִפְתַּח אִישׁ בּוֹר אוֹ כִּי יִכְרֶה אִישׁ בּוֹר ("and if a man opens a pit, or if a man digs a pit"), and His saying at the end of the account [Exod 21:34] כֶּסֶף יָשִׁיב לִבְעָלָיו וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לּוֹ ("he shall restore money to its owner, and the dead [beast] shall be his"). Yet not everything that falls into the pit dies; rather, a fracture or a defect may befall it, so that a measure of loss becomes due [for it]. [Scripture] mentioned nothing of that; rather it mentioned the final and uttermost case, which is death — and that when the whole is gone, the restoration of its like becomes obligatory upon him. So the need compelled [recourse] to the employment of analogy (qiyās) for what falls short of that: that if a defect with a known measure of loss befalls [the beast], the like of that becomes obligatory in it — namely that [the offender] gives a sound [animal] and takes the broken and defective one, just as, when death occurred, he gave its replacement and himself took the dead one. And the like of that is His saying [Exod 22:6] כִּי יִתֵּן אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ כֶּסֶף אוֹ כֵּלִים לִשְׁמוֹר ("if a man gives to his fellow money or vessels to keep") etc. — and he did not mention gold that is not a vessel; and this is like the first [case].

: This unmarked paragraph (Nemoy's first numbered marker is "3," at the head of §3) is a methodological bridge, not yet about eschatology. It illustrates Q's Karaite doctrine of qiyās (legal analogy): Scripture legislates only the limit-case (the beast that dies in the pit; the vessels given in deposit) and leaves the intermediate cases (a beast merely injured; a deposit of unworked gold) to be derived by analogy. This is laid down here to license the interpretive move the whole bab depends on — that the Torah states its eschatology tersely and by limit-case ("you shall surely die"), leaving its full doctrinal content to be drawn out by sound inference and by the later prophets. The principle is the Karaite counterpart to (and rival of) Rabbanite hekkesh/gezerah shawah; Q grounds it not in tradition but in the economy of the scriptural text itself.
§3 — Eden and the tree of life: "you shall surely die" means expulsion from the abode of life

Since we have set forth what we have set forth of that, let us take up the exposition of what we intended — the indication, from Scripture, [bearing] upon what is in the hands of all people: the mention of the Garden (al-janna), which is the abode of the righteous and the dwelling of the pious. We say that we have found Him saying [Gen 2:8-9] וַיִּטַּע יְיָ אֱלֹהִים גַּן בְּעֵדֶן מִקֶּדֶם ("the Lord God planted a garden in Eden, eastward"), and its completion וַיַּצְמַח יְיָ אֱלֹהִים from the ground כָּל עֵץ נֶחְמָד ("the Lord God caused to grow … every pleasant tree"), and its completion וְנָהָר יוֹצֵא מֵעֵדֶן ("and a river went out of Eden") etc., to the end of the account; and He says [Gen 2:15] וַיִּקַּח יְיָ אֱלֹהִים אֶת הָאָדָם וַיַּנִּחֵהוּ ("the Lord God took the man and set him") etc.; then He sealed the account by His saying [Gen 2:17] כִּי בְּיוֹם אֲכָלְךָ מִמֶּנּוּ מוֹת תָּמוּת ("for on the day you eat of it you shall surely die") etc.

The first thing the one who ponders this account needs is to know that Adam and Eve, when they ate, did not die on the day they ate — only that they came to be mortal (ṣārā yamūtān). Then He said after that [Gen 3:22] וְעַתָּה פֶּן יִשְׁלַח יָדוֹ וְלָקַח גַּם מֵעֵץ הַחַיִּים וְאָכַל וָחַי לְעוֹלָם ("and now, lest he put forth his hand and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live forever"), and He said [Gen 3:23] וַיְשַׁלְּחֵהוּ יְיָ אֱלֹהִים מִגַּן עֵדֶן ("and the Lord God sent him forth from the Garden of Eden"). So this statement indicated that the soil from which he was created is the soil of that which is outside the Garden, [and that this] is not of the soil of the Garden. And He also said in [Gen 3:19] כִּי בְּזֵעַת אַפֶּךָ תֹּאכַל לֶחֶם עַד שׁוּבְךָ אֶל הָאֲדָמָה כִּי מִמֶּנָּה לֻקָּחְתָּ ("by the sweat of your brow shall you eat bread, until you return to the ground, for from it you were taken") — so by these two statements He indicated that it is from the ground outside the Garden that Adam was created, and to it he returns (that is, at his death), and that this ground outside the Garden is a thing of death (dhāt mawt).

So it became plain from this that the meaning of His saying [Gen 2:17] כִּי בְּיוֹם אֲכָלְךָ מִמֶּנּוּ מוֹת תָּמוּת is: "you shall be expelled from the abode of life and shall come to be in the abode from which you were taken and to which you return — and it is the abode of death." Then He said [Gen 3:24] וַיְגָרֶשׁ אֶת הָאָדָם ("and He drove out the man"). So this — together with His saying [Gen 3:22] וָחַי לְעוֹלָם, and together with the angels' guarding of the Garden against him whom Adam would [otherwise] enter — indicated that His saying מוֹת תָּמוּת means that one who dies neither dwells in it nor enters it, [namely] one who is barred from eating of the tree of life; and that none takes refuge in it save one who eats of the tree of life and lives the eternal life (al-ḥayāh al-abadiyya).

: The keystone exegesis of the bab. Q reads the Eden narrative against the surface objection — "but Adam did not die on the day he ate" — and converts it into the doctrine: mot tamut does not predict same-day biological death but a change of abode, from the deathless Garden (the soil and the tree of life are inside) to the mortal ground (from which Adam was made, and to which he returns) outside. The argument is built entirely from the text's own seams: the soil Adam tills and returns to (Gen 3:19, 3:23) is explicitly outside the Garden, so the "death" of the sentence is exile to the realm of death. The angels' guarding of the way to the tree of life (Gen 3:24) is read teleologically — see §4. This is the Karaite ẓāhir-anchored reading turned to eschatological purpose: the Garden becomes the type of the otherworldly thawāb.
§4 — The guarded tree cannot be purposeless: the Garden awaits the obedient

(4.) There is no doubt that all the people of this world die of necessity; and for this reason the world came to be not an abode of life but an abode of death. And since one who dies does not enter the Garden, [it follows that] all the people of the world do not enter it; and the angels' guarding of it indicates that it is made ready and prepared for one who [shall] enter it and eat of the tree of life and live the eternal life. For if it were not so, then it — and the angels' guarding of it — would be without cause; and there is nothing in God's creation (mighty and exalted) that is so, for He is far above frivolity (al-ʿabath). And He informed concerning the angels that they guard the way of the tree of life; and a fruit-bearing tree [meant] for no eating from it has no meaning and no [point to its] persistence. So inevitably He is only awaiting, for it, those who [shall] eat from it — and they are the people of the eternal life. And in Adam's [continued] standing in it at his obedience, and his expulsion from it at his disobedience, there is an indication that this is the way of the rest of his offspring: that whoever among them obeys is deserving of entry into it (mustaḥiqqan li-l-dukhūl), and whoever disobeys does not deserve that. So this is a clear indication of the Garden, which is the abode of the people of obedience, who eat of the tree of life and so live the eternal life; and it is not for the people of the world, who die and do not enter it. And its persistence is made ready for him whose way is this; and the people of disobedience are expelled from it. So even were there in [the matter of] otherworldly reward no indication other than this, it would [still] suffice; and how much more so, when we shall bring of that many proofs!

: The "no purposeless creation" argument is a kalāmī ḥikma-axiom (God does not act in vain, yataʿālā ʿan al-ʿabath) put to exegetical work: a guarded, fruit-bearing, never-to-be-eaten tree would be pointless — therefore the Garden must be awaiting future eaters, namely the eschatologically obedient. Adam's tenure-on-obedience / expulsion-on-disobedience is then read typologically as the rule for all his offspring: istiḥqāq (desert) of the Garden is conditioned on obedience. istiḥqāq (here "deserving / desert") is the Bahshamī technical term for the merited basis of reward and punishment (glossary §VI); this is its first substantive occurrence in the bab.
§5 — Deut 6:24-25: two distinct goods — "all the days" (this world) and "to keep us alive as this day" (the next)

(.5) And we need here to make plain that the one who enters it, of those who have this description, is he who in this world was of those who live after their death (man yaḥyā baʿda mawtihi), of the people of obedience — and they are the people of the world-to-come (ahl al-ākhira). He says in the Torah [Deut 6:20] כִּי יִשְׁאָלְךָ בִּנְךָ מָחָר לֵאמֹר מָה הָעֵדֹת וְהַחֻקִּים [וְהַמִּשְׁפָּטִים אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְיָ אֱלֹהֵינוּ אֶתְכֶם], [Deut 6:24] וַיְצַוֵּנוּ יְיָ לַעֲשׂוֹת אֶת כָּל הַחֻקִּים הָאֵלֶּה לְיִרְאָה אֶת יְיָ אֱלֹהֵינוּ לְטוֹב לָנוּ כָּל הַיָּמִים, and its completion [Deut 6:24-25] לְחַיֹּתֵנוּ כְּהַיּוֹם הַזֶּה וּצְדָקָה תִּהְיֶה לָּנוּ כִּי נִשְׁמֹר לַעֲשׂוֹת אֶת כָּל הַחֻקִּים הָאֵלֶּה ("to keep us alive, as it is this day; and it shall be righteousness for us, if we observe to do all these ordinances"), and its completion.

So He informed of two parts, one of which precedes the other, the other following the first. The first is His saying לְטוֹב לָנוּ כָּל הַיָּמִים ("for our good, all the days"), which are the lifetime of this world; and the second is His saying לְחַיֹּתֵנוּ כְּהַיּוֹם הַזֶּה ("to keep us alive, as this day") — which inevitably [comes] after it, and which is another recompense and an otherworldly life (ḥayāh ākhiriyya), its meaning being the meaning of life after death. And one who lives after his death must inevitably have an abode and a homeland; and it cannot rightly be that his abode is this world, since the [first] statement fell upon what is after "all the days," which are the time of this world. So when the time of this world has elapsed, the time of death has elapsed and the time of life has set in — except that the earth of this world remains in it, [though] not its [former] time; and the place of the dead remains. And we shall expound this statement hereafter.

: The first lexical proof from the Torah itself. Q parses Deut 6:24-25 as naming two distinct goods in sequence: (a) "for our good, all the days" = the temporal welfare of this world; and (b) "to keep us alive, as this day" = a further recompense, the otherworldly life after "all the days." The argument is structural: since clause (b) is appended after the clause covering the entire span of worldly days, it cannot itself denote worldly life — it must denote post-mortem life, the ḥayāh ākhiriyya (otherworldly life). This is the textual hook for the bab's governing thesis (that Torah "life" = otherworldly reward). The verse-pointer in the source ("Deut 6:6, 6:20") is garbled in the OCR; the citation is Deut 6:20-25.
§6 — God's recompense must be complete, hence eternal; the eaters of the tree dwell in the Garden

(.6) So it is established that the abode of one who lives [again] is the world-to-come; and since they live only for the recompense, and it is of the manner of the recompense of the Maker (mighty and exalted) that it be complete (tāmm) — and the complete is that which does not fall short of eternity (al-abadiyya), else there would be between it and eternity a defect (naqḍ), and the recompense of God (mighty and exalted) is not defective — their life, then, which they live after all their worldly days, and after the beneficence shown to them therein, is eternal. And the like of these — to them befits the eating of the tree of life, and their dwelling-place is where it is; and it is in the Garden, so their dwelling-place is inevitably in the Garden made ready for them and guarded. All the more so, since Scripture has conjoined the statement that comprised beneficence and good in all the days, and life altogether like these days — which is [Deut 6:24-25] וּלְטוֹב לָנוּ כָּל הַיָּמִים לְחַיֹּתֵנוּ כְּהַיּוֹם הַזֶּה — just as He says of the people of life נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים ("the breath of life"); and its precision is for [both] this world and its completion, and [that] we become righteous before God our God. So inevitably the Garden is the dwelling of the righteous and the pure. And this is sufficient in this matter; yet we [now] make it plain from another aspect — and that too is from the Torah, and the interpretation of it from the words of the saints (al-awliyāʾ).

: The kalāmī premise made explicit: God's recompense must be tāmm (complete/perfect), and a recompense that "falls short of eternity" would be defective (naqḍ) — therefore the reward of the obedient must be eternal (abadī). This is the taʾbīd (eternalization) doctrine (glossary §VI): perfection of divine justice entails the perpetuity of reward. The argument is a priori (from the concept of divine recompense), buttressing the textual argument of §5. The OCR of the back half is rough; the gist — the conjunction of worldly "good" and otherworldly "life" in Deut 6:24-25, glossed by nishmat ḥayyim (Gen 2:7), proves the Garden is the righteous' dwelling — is secure. "al-awliyāʾ" (the saints / friends-of-God) is Q's term for the prophets whose later expositions §7 adduces.
§7 — Solomon and David interpret the Torah: the soul survives, and body-and-soul are reunited for reward

(7.) We say that Scripture said [Gen 2:7] וַיִּיצֶר יְיָ אֱלֹהִים אֶת הָאָדָם עָפָר from the ground וַיִּפַּח בְּאַפָּיו נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים ("the Lord God formed the man, dust from the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life") and its completion. And שְׁלֹמֹה (peace be upon him) came with the interpretation of God's saying to Adam [Gen 3:19] בְּזֵעַת אַפֶּךָ תֹּאכַל לֶחֶם עַד שׁוּבְךָ אֶל הָאֲדָמָה ("by the sweat of your brow shall you eat bread, until you return to the ground"), and the philosopher [Solomon] said in [Eccl 12:7] וְיָשֹׁב הֶעָפָר עַל הָאָרֶץ כְּשֶׁהָיָה וְהָרוּחַ תָּשׁוּב אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים אֲשֶׁר נְתָנָהּ ("and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it"). So he made known to us the persistence of the spirit (baqāʾ al-rūḥ) after its separation from the body, and that it does not perish nor pass away, and that it is not of the accidents (al-aʿrāḍ) but is of the living substances (al-jawāhir al-ḥayya). This, then, is the saying of שְׁלֹמֹה.

Then דָּוִד (peace be upon him) interpreted the Torah's saying [Deut 6:24-25] וּלְטוֹב לָנוּ כָּל הַיָּמִים לְחַיֹּתֵנוּ כְּהַיּוֹם הַזֶּה by his saying [Ps 104:29] תֹּסֵף רוּחָם יִגְוָעוּן וְאֶל עֲפָרָם יְשׁוּבוּן ("You gather in their spirit, they expire and return to their dust"); then he said [Ps 104:30] תְּשַׁלַּח רוּחֲךָ יִבָּרֵאוּן וּתְחַדֵּשׁ פְּנֵי אֲדָמָה ("You send forth Your spirit, they are created, and You renew the face of the ground"). So [Solomon] informed — peace be upon him — of the persistence of the spirit after the bodies; and דָּוִד informed that God sends it [back] into their bodies, and the face of the ground is renewed: so the bodies, in their very selves, are brought to life by their spirits, until they return as they were — not the spirits without the bodies, nor the bodies without the spirits, but rather the recompense attaches to the whole, spirit and body.

And all this, in accordance with what we have said, is an interpretation of what is in the Torah, of His saying [Deut 6:24-25] לְטוֹב לָנוּ כָּל הַיָּמִים לְחַיֹּתֵנוּ כְּהַיּוֹם הַזֶּה and His saying וּלְצְדָקָה תִּהְיֶה לָּנוּ ("and it shall be righteousness for us"). For they [the speakers of that verse] did not say that while being bodies and spirits together, except that what is restored and brought-to-life is body and spirit together — just as the beneficence in this world was to them both together, since He says לְטוֹב לָנוּ כָּל הַיָּמִים לְחַיֹּתֵנוּ — so likewise the life is to them both together, and the recompense to them [both], not to one of them without the other. So once what we have said has become plain, then: one who does not live the otherworldly life of the Garden is in his place in the abode of death; and since that is so, and those days are otherworldly, not worldly, then they are [thus] in the abode of their punishment — just as the one who lives for the Garden, for him the Garden is the abode of his life.

: The resurrection doctrine, derived by reading the later prophets as commentators on the Torah. Solomon (Eccl 12:7) supplies the survival of the spirit (here argued in kalāmī terms: the rūḥ is not an accident, ʿaraḍ, but a persisting jawhar ḥayy, a living substance — so it does not perish at bodily death). David (Ps 104:29-30) supplies the re-embodiment: the spirit is sent back into "their bodies," which are revived "in their very selves" (bi-aʿyānihā). The polemical payoff against any spiritualizing (or merely-this-worldly) reading is that the iʿāda (restoration/resurrection) is of body-and-soul together, because the obedience that earned reward was a joint act of body and soul. This bicompartmental resurrection (full body-soul reward in the Garden; later disembodied soul-reward in al-dahr) is developed in §§20-23.
§8 — Death and life are paired with evil and good; the worldly and otherworldly senses run parallel

(8.) And among what the Torah also informed concerning both classes — I mean the living [and the dead] … [lacuna] … and good is the opposite of evil. So since this world was the abode of one who dies, and is the abode of death, it could not be that the life mentioned here is the life of this world — since this world is not the abode of life; for when He conjoined the good with the life, that conformed to what had preceded, of the mention of what is in the reply to those who say [Deut 6:24-25] בְּדָבָר וכד׳ לְטוֹב לָנוּ כָּל הַיָּמִים לְחַיֹּתֵנוּ כְּהַיּוֹם הַזֶּה. The good conjoined with the life — for the bodies that perform the duty — is the recompense of this world; and the bare [unconjoined] life is an otherworldly, eternal life. And so [death and evil] came to be set opposite [life and good], they being death and evil; one of them too — that is, the worldly one of them — is worldly, and [the one] opposite the otherworldly is otherworldly. Then He said, a little after that [Deut 30:19] בְּשֵׁם יְיָ … הַעִדֹתִי [בָכֶם] הַיּוֹם אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֶת הָאָרֶץ הַחַיִּים וְהַמָּוֶת נָתַתִּי לְפָנֶיךָ הַבְּרָכָה וְהַקְּלָלָה ("I call to witness against you this day the heavens and the earth: I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse").

: The verse straddles the §7/§8 page-break and the OCR shows a short lacuna at the head of §8 (the apodosis of "among what the Torah also informed concerning both classes" is lost). The reconstructed argument: Deut 30:19 pairs life/death with blessing/curse (= good/evil), and since "death" patently cannot mean ordinary worldly death (which befalls righteous and wicked alike — the point §10 will press), the life and death here must run on two parallel registers, a worldly sense (welfare/affliction) and an otherworldly sense (reward/punishment). The pairing of the two oppositions (life:death :: good:evil), each split into worldly and otherworldly senses, is the formal core of the lexical thesis.
§9 — Solomon proves this world is no abode of recompense; "life and good" in Deut 30:15 are otherworldly

So the true life does not fall upon the life of this world, since it perishes and passes away and death succeeds it, and since it may comprise the righteous and the wicked alike — so much so that there may be a wicked man whose life is longer than the life of the righteous. And since it cannot be that the recompense is of this character, for this reason Solomon (peace be upon him) said [Eccl 7:15] אֶת הַכֹּל רָאִיתִי בִּימֵי הֶבְלִי יֵשׁ צַדִּיק אֹבֵד בְּצִדְקוֹ וְיֵשׁ רָשָׁע מַאֲרִיךְ בְּרָעָתוֹ ("all this I saw in the days of my vanity: there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and a wicked man who prolongs [his life] in his evil"). So Solomon's saying invalidates the statement of whoever claims that the Torah held out incentive only to the goods of this world — since he was a Hebrew man holding the view of the Hebrews, and this is in accordance with their saying. And Solomon also said another saying, the counterpart of this saying we have mentioned, namely his saying [Eccl 8:14] אֲשֶׁר יֵשׁ צַדִּיקִים שֶׁמַּגִּיעַ אֲלֵיהֶם כְּמַעֲשֵׂה הָרְשָׁעִים וְיֵשׁ רְשָׁעִים שֶׁמַּגִּיעַ אֲלֵיהֶם כְּמַעֲשֵׂה הַצַּדִּיקִים ("that there are righteous men to whom it happens according to the deeds of the wicked, and wicked men to whom it happens according to the deeds of the righteous") — he meant that in existence there are righteous men whom there touches what the deeds of the wicked merit, and wicked men whom there touches what the deeds of the righteous merit; so he said: this is a world of vapor (ʿālam al-habāʾ)! How, then, with this [before him], could it be admissible for a claimant to claim that our scriptures hold out incentive only to the worldly goods — when Solomon's statement declares explicitly that this world is not an abode of recompense?

(9.) So we say: since Solomon has barred this world from being an abode of recompense, then inevitably his saying in the Torah [Deut 30:15] רְאֵה נָתַתִּי לְפָנֶיךָ הַיּוֹם אֶת הַחַיִּים וְאֶת הַטּוֹב ("see, I have set before you this day life and good") did not intend by it the life of this world nor its death, and likewise its good and its evil; rather he intended by it the latter life and the latter death (al-ḥayāh al-akhīra wa-l-mawt al-akhīr). Then Moses (peace be upon him) also expounded that and interpreted it, and informed of the reward, and who is the one deserving of the reward — he who is fit for the dwelling of the Garden and the eating of the tree of life within it — and who it is that did not deserve that, but rather his dwelling shall be the abode of death, which is the earth …

: Q recruits Qohelet as a Hebrew witness against the "this-worldly-reward-only" thesis (whether held by Christian polemicists or by Jewish literalists): Eccl 7:15 and 8:14 observe that worldly fortune is not correlated with desert (righteous perish, wicked prosper) — "this is a world of vapor" (ʿālam al-habāʾ, glossing Qohelet's hevel). If worldly outcome does not track righteousness, then the Torah's promise of "life and good" (Deut 30:15) cannot be worldly; it must be the latter life and death — i.e., otherworldly reward and punishment. The argument's force is that it is mounted from within the canon (Solomon "a Hebrew holding the Hebrews' view"), pre-empting the charge that otherworldly eschatology is a foreign import.
§10 — Ezekiel's "second death": the dead cannot die again, so it is otherworldly punishment

… from which Adam was created and to which he returned, and upon which the human beings died, and from which the righteous and pious are removed: God (exalted) brings them to the abode of life, which is the Garden.

(10.) So we say that the righteous (al-barr) and the wicked (al-fājir) are two extremes, neither of which deserves its name save by the conjunction of the things that יְחֶזְקֵאל the prophet (peace be upon him) mentions in his interpretation of what we have mentioned of what is in the Torah. For he said [Ezek 18:5-6] כִּי יִהְיֶה צַדִּיק וְעָשָׂה מִשְׁפָּט וּצְדָקָה אֶל הֶהָרִים לֹא אָכַל ("if a man be righteous and do justice and righteousness, [and] has not eaten upon the mountains") and the rest of what is after that, to the end of the account; and he said at its end [Ezek 18:9] בְּחֻקּוֹתַי יְהַלֵּךְ וּמִשְׁפָּטַי שָׁמַר לַעֲשׂוֹת אֱמֶת צַדִּיק הוּא חָיֹה יִחְיֶה ("he walks in My statutes and has kept My ordinances to do truth — he is righteous; he shall surely live"). Then he enumerated the deeds of the wicked, saying [Ezek 18:10] וְהוֹלִיד בֵּן פָּרִיץ שֹׁפֵךְ דָּם ("and he begets a violent son, a shedder of blood") and the whole account, which is the opposite of what he described in the righteous, and said [Ezek 18:13] גַּם לֹא יִחְיֶה אֵת כָּל הַתּוֹעֵבוֹת הָאֵלֶּה עָשָׂה מוֹת יוּמָת דָּמָיו בּוֹ יִהְיֶה ("he shall surely not live; he has done all these abominations, he shall surely be put to death, his blood shall be upon him"). So these two divisions are the two extremes in righteousness and wickedness, each of which contradicts its fellow and removes it and effaces it, by reason of their mutual contrariety and contradiction.

Then יְחֶזְקֵאל (peace be upon him) did not leave what he mentioned of death and life until he had spoken plainly of his meaning in them and informed of his intent — that being in his saying [Ezek 18:26] וּבְשׁוּב צַדִּיק מִצִּדְקָתוֹ וְעָשָׂה עָוֶל וּמֵת עֲלֵיהֶם ("and when a righteous man turns from his righteousness and does iniquity, and dies for them") — and this is inevitably the immediate [worldly] death (al-mawt al-ʿājil); then he said [Ezek 18:27] וּבְשׁוּב רָשָׁע מֵרִשְׁעָתוֹ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה etc. יִחְיֶה ("and when a wicked man turns from his wickedness which he did … he shall live"). So he mentioned a second death after the first death of which he said וּמֵת עֲלֵיהֶם — and it became clear from this that by mentioning the second death he intended the latter death, which is after the death of this world, and that is the punishment (al-ʿiqāb). For otherwise — how does the dead man die after his death? So it is established that the meaning of life and death, and their force, in the Hebrew language is reward and punishment. This is attested from the standpoint of language, and attested from the standpoint of sense [experience]; and the rational [point] is that the Sage (al-ḥakīm) cannot inform of a thing whose contrary is observed. So since He has informed that the righteous lives and does not die, and the wicked dies and does not live, and we used to see many righteous men [who] die …

: The philological master-stroke of the bab. Ezekiel 18 first defines the two extremes (the wholly righteous "shall surely live"; the wholly wicked "shall surely be put to death"), then — crucially — speaks of a second death: the apostate righteous man "dies for them" (Ezek 18:26, the ordinary worldly death), and yet the wicked who repents "shall live." Q's logical lever: a dead man cannot die again — so when Scripture predicates "death" of one who has already died the worldly death, that second "death" must be the otherworldly punishment. This proves, "from the standpoint of language," that Hebrew ḥayāh/mawt carry the technical force thawāb/ʿiqāb. The "rational" rider invokes the kalāmī axiom that the Sage (al-ḥakīm = God) does not assert what observation contradicts (the obviously-mortal righteous), forcing the non-literal reading. The sentence runs over the page-break into §11.
§11 — "You shall not die" (to David) and "let Reuben live" confirm death = otherworldly punishment; repentance and apostasy

… they die — so it became established beyond doubt that by this life and this death He did not intend the immediate, observed life and death, but rather some other death and life were intended, namely reward and punishment. And this is the very wording of what the Torah said, in [Deut 30:15] רְאֵה נָתַתִּי לְפָנֶיךָ הַיּוֹם אֶת הַחַיִּים וְאֶת הַמָּוֶת אֶת הַטּוֹב וְאֶת הָרָע ("see, I have set before you this day the life and the death, the good and the evil").

(11.) And among what corroborates what we have said — also — of [the fact] that this word, I mean death, may fall in the Hebrew tongue upon punishment, is the saying of [Nathan to David, 2 Sam 12:13] גַּם יְיָ הֶעֱבִיר חַטָּאתְךָ לֹא תָמוּת ("the Lord also has put away your sin; you shall not die") — yet we have seen that he [David] did die; so inevitably he informed him only that the punishment of the world-to-come (ʿiqāb al-ākhira) would not overtake him. The like of that is the saying of Moses (peace be upon him) [Deut 33:6] יְחִי רְאוּבֵן וְאַל יָמֹת ("let Reuben live and not die") — since [Reuben] had turned back and repented and did not die upon his disobedience, the punishment of the world-to-come was remitted from him; and that is according to what יְחֶזְקֵאל (peace be upon him) expounded. And also [a corroboration is] that whoever turns back from his righteousness and dies a transgressor comes to be in the punishment, and what preceded of his righteousness does not avail him; and likewise whoever turns back from his transgression and dies righteous comes to be in the reward, and what preceded of his transgression does not harm him — that being in His saying [Ezek 18:24] וּבְשׁוּב צַדִּיק מִצִּדְקָתוֹ וְעָשָׂה עָוֶל ("and when a righteous man turns from his righteousness and does iniquity") and the whole account, and His saying [Ezek 18:27] וּבְשׁוּב רָשָׁע מֵרִשְׁעָתוֹ ("and when a wicked man turns from his wickedness") to the completion of the two accounts.

And in this matter there is a question (masʾala) which I shall mention at the end of the discussion, and I shall mention what ought to be said concerning it — except that Scripture made known to us that the penitent is requited (yuqtaṣṣu minhu) in this world for what he committed, and that is known from the account of דָּוִד (peace be upon him): אַבְשָׁלוֹם was set over him, and in that was an expiation (tamḥīṣ) for what passed from him with the wife of אוּרִיָּה; so the reward, together with sincere repentance (al-tawba al-naṣūḥ), was made clear to him, and the otherworldly punishment was passed over from him — and that is His saying לֹא תָמוּת.

: Two further philological proofs that mawt = otherworldly punishment, both turning on figures who manifestly did die a natural death: (a) Nathan tells David "you shall not die" (2 Sam 12:13) after the Bathsheba affair — yet David died, so the spared "death" is the otherworldly one; (b) Moses blesses "let Reuben live and not die" (Deut 33:6) — Reuben, having repented, is spared otherworldly death. Q introduces the doctrines of tawba (repentance), this-worldly qiṣāṣ/tamḥīṣ (requital/expiation — David punished by Absalom's revolt), and the apostasy/repentance reversibility of Ezek 18:24-27 (final state determines reward). The "question I shall mention at the end" is the iḥbāṭ/takfīr problem (the cancellation of prior merit by later sin and vice versa) flagged here and engaged in §§13-15b.
§12 — The Garden's delights, and Ezekiel's "you were in Eden" addressed to Adam

(12.) So we have now informed and indicated that the otherworldly life is the descent into the Garden and the dwelling in it, and the enjoyment in it of the sweetness of its fruits, the marvels of its tastes, the beauty of its sights, and the fragrance of its scents, and the partaking of the eternal life by eating of the tree of life that gives security from death, and the joy of the soul in that, and in what is in it of domes (qibāb) of gold and jewel and ruby — red and yellow — and lapis-lazuli (al-ismānjūnī) and the like of that, such as emerald and other [stones]. We know that from the account of יְחֶזְקֵאל in his rebuke of the king of Tyre, when he says [Ezek 28:13] בְּעֵדֶן גַּן אֱלֹהִים הָיִיתָ כָּל אֶבֶן יְקָרָה מְסֻכָתֶךָ אֹדֶם פִּטְדָה וְיַהֲלֹם תַּרְשִׁישׁ שֹׁהַם וְיָשְׁפֵה סַפִּיר נֹפֶךְ וּבָרֶקַת וְזָהָב ("you were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone was your covering — carnelian, topaz, and diamond, beryl, onyx, and jasper, sapphire, turquoise, and emerald, and gold"). And he had earlier put forward the statement to him, saying [Ezek 28:12] חוֹתֵם תָּכְנִית — that is, "are you the seal of the form?" — meaning by that Adam, who was the seal of creation; then he followed that with his saying בְּעֵדֶן גַּן אֱלֹהִים הָיִיתָ ("you were in Eden, the garden of God"), since Adam dwelt in this Garden which has within it these domes that are of gold and the [various] kinds of jewels.

: A sensory portrait of the thawāb of the Garden, grounded in Ezekiel's dirge over the king of Tyre (Ezek 28:12-13). Q reads the addressee not as the Tyrian king simpliciter but, through ḥotem toknit ("seal of the form/design"), as Adam — "the seal of creation" who really was "in Eden, the garden of God" — making the gem-studded Eden of the dirge a literal description of the Garden's reward. The catalogue of stones is reproduced as Q gives it; al-ismānjūnī (lapis-lazuli / azure) glosses sappir. The reading of the Tyre-dirge's Eden as the real reward-Garden is a distinctively Karaite literalizing move.
§13 — Prior sin is canceled by repentance, and prior obedience by apostasy: the hundred-years problem

(13.) We return to the mention of the question that is in His saying וַיָּשׁוֹב יְיָ … וּבְשׁוּב צַדִּיק [and His saying] נָשׁוּב … וְנָשׁוּב [the shuv verbs of turning]. So we say that He informed that what is past of disobediences does not harm [one] upon repentance and turning-back; and likewise what is past of acts of obedience does not avail [one] upon apostasy. So there followed from that [the case] that if a man profaned the Sabbath a hundred years and more, then repented and turned back and kept a single Sabbath and then died — all that he had profaned of those Sabbaths would be forgiven him; and likewise if he had broken the fast of כִּפּוּר (the Day of Atonement) a hundred years, then repented and fasted a single כִּפּוּר; and likewise all the disobediences. And likewise, too, if he fasted כִּפּוּר a hundred years as God commanded, and observed the Sabbath as was made obligatory upon him, together with all the acts of obedience, then profaned a single Sabbath and broke the fast of a single כִּפּוּר — he would have squandered all that preceded of fasting and of observing the Sabbaths.

So let whoever would ask, ask, saying: why is that obligatory — when he had obeyed a hundred years and toiled and wearied his soul in seeking God (mighty and exalted), and abandoned that a single time — that all he had toiled and labored in should be squandered, when his abandoning of it on that one occasion was not by way of unbelief (kufr) nor by way of denial (takdhīb), but rather …

: Q now raises the iḥbāṭ / takfīr problem (cancellation and expiation of works) — a central Bahshamī controversy. The reversibility doctrine of Ezek 18 (final-state determines destiny: prior sin erased by repentance, prior merit erased by apostasy) yields a hard case: a single late Sabbath-profanation or Yom-Kippur-breaking apparently annuls a century of obedience. The objector's complaint — that it seems unjust to void a lifetime of toil for one lapse not amounting to kufr (unbelief) or takdhīb (denial) — sets up the qualified answer of §§14-15a. (kufr / takdhīb are the standard kalāmī limit-conditions; mere transgression without disbelief is the disputed middle case.)
§14 — The answer of "some of the people of inquiry": cancellation applies only where there is denial and regret

… that was for the seeking of a pleasure, or an ease, or a desire for some immediate matter, or a dread of missing something present, or the befalling of something hateful — whether in a small matter or a large — while he is withal acknowledging and confessing that what he did was an act of error, and that he is committing a sin, abandoning what is obligatory and binding. So can it be that one whose way is this should squander all that he wearied and toiled his soul in throughout his lifetime, so that there is no difference between him and one who did not toil and labor, but was rather immersed in disobediences his whole life long? And is this of the description of justice (al-ʿadl)?

(14.) So we say that some of the people of inquiry (baʿḍ ahl al-naẓar) have gone, in that, to a view that we approve and adopt — for it is a view that issues in justice and excludes wrong (al-jawr), and distinguishes between one who has worked and toiled and one who has not worked and labored and toiled. He claimed that the saying of Scripture [Prov 24:16] כִּי שֶׁבַע יִפֹּל [צַדִּיק] וָקָם וְחָשׁוּב צַדִּיק ("for [though] the righteous fall seven times, he rises [and is] reckoned righteous") is not a statement [made] absolutely, in every respect, but rather is bound up with another thing — namely that the one who abandoned that abandoned it only by way of denial (takdhīb) and regret over what he did, and the belief that what he had been keeping up throughout that period was vain and a vapor, of no meaning, and was not [really] obligatory upon him, and that he toiled and labored for [mere] wind. He said: and that is the counterpart of the penitent from disobediences — for those disobediences of his are not mentioned [against him] and the punishment is voided from him only when he is regretful for what he did of them, confessing that he was in error, abandoning what is obligatory. And that is like one who profaned the Sabbath a hundred years and repented while he is acknowledging that he was in disobedience and at variance with the Creator (mighty and exalted): for by that [acknowledgment] it is forgiven him, and his profanation of those Sabbaths is voided from him — as the prophet (peace be upon him) said [Ezek 18:23 / 18:32] לֹא אֶחְפֹּץ בְּמוֹת הָרָשָׁע כִּי אִם בְּשׁוּב רָשָׁע מִדַּרְכּוֹ וְחָיָה ("I do not desire the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked turn from his way and live") and its completion; and He said [Joel 2:12] שׁוּבוּ עָדַי בְּכָל לְבַבְכֶם ("turn back to Me with all your heart") and the rest of the passage; and He said [Joel 2:14] מִי יוֹדֵעַ יָשׁוּב וְנִחָם ("who knows whether He will turn and relent") and its completion; and He said [Mal 3:7] שׁוּבוּ אֵלַי וְאָשׁוּבָה אֲלֵיכֶם ("turn back to Me, and I will turn back to you") and its completion; and He said [Jer 16:19] גּוֹיִם יָבֹאוּ מֵאַפְסֵי אָרֶץ וְיֹאמְרוּ אַךְ שֶׁקֶר נָחֲלוּ אֲבוֹתֵינוּ ("nations shall come from the ends of the earth and say: our fathers inherited only falsehood") and its completion. And the two cases together are equivalent: each of the two parties has voided [for him] only what preceded of his work — be it obedience or disobedience — at the [point of] abandonment, when there is, withal, denial and regret and the belief that what passed from him …

: The resolution Q endorses (attributed to "some of the people of inquiry," baʿḍ ahl al-naẓar — i.e., the Bahshamī-aligned Karaite mutakallimūn). The iḥbāṭ (cancellation) of prior merit is not unconditional: Prov 24:16 ("the righteous falls seven times and rises") is glossed as qualified — a lapse cancels a lifetime's obedience only if it is accompanied by takdhīb (repudiation) and nadam (regret), i.e., the apostate's belief that his prior devotion was worthless. The symmetry is exact: just as the penitent sinner's prior sins are voided because he now repudiates and regrets them, so the apostate's prior merits are voided because he now repudiates and regrets them. Mere lapse without repudiation does not trigger cancellation — securing al-ʿadl (justice) against the objection of §13. The chain of "return" prooftexts (Ezek 18, Joel 2, Mal 3, Jer 16) grounds the doctrine of tawba. The "utmāmuhu"/"wa-qāl" markers in the source are partly Arabicized Hebrew incipits; rendered as citation-tags.
§15a — The ground of the doctrine: be-yad ramah (Num 15:30) is defiant, contemptuous transgression, not every inadvertent sin

… had no meaning. And this, in our view, is a sound doctrine, and a view that justice (al-ʿadl) necessitates and that leads to justice. And it is the counterpart of what He says in Scripture [Num 15:30] נֶפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר תַּעֲשֶׂה בְּיָד רָמָה מִן הָאֶזְרָח ("the soul that acts with a high hand, of the native-born") and its completion כו׳ כִּי דְבַר יְיָ בָּזָה ("[because] he has despised the word of the Lord") and its completion — whose meaning is not what some people imagine, namely that He intended that everyone who commits any sin whatever, deliberately, must be put to death — whatever sin it be — since that would be absurd, for one who steals is not liable to death but is liable [only] to a twofold restitution, and the like of that is much. He meant by His saying בְּיָד רָמָה only one who does that with arrogance and overbearing power (bi-tajabbur wa-qtidār) and contempt for the duty, and with the belief that for what he does there is no accountability against him and no otherworldly punishment — for He says of him כִּי דְבַר יְיָ בָּזָה, and says [Num 15:31] כִּי דְבַר יְיָ בָּזָה ("for he has despised the word of the Lord"). So know by that that this is the one who scorns and makes light and holds in contempt, to the exclusion of others — except for that which the text [explicitly] specified that he is put to death for, such as gross immorality, the profaning of the Sabbath, and the like of that.

: The doctrinal anchor for the qualified-cancellation view: Num 15:30-31's "be-yad ramah" ("with a high hand") sinner. Q (with the inquiry-folk) reads it not as "any deliberate sin" (which would absurdly make theft a capital crime, when the Torah prescribes mere double restitution) but as the defiant, contemptuous transgressor who "despises the word of the Lord" — one who acts bi-tajabbur (with arrogance) believing there is no otherworldly accountability. This is the same disposition (takdhīb + contempt) that triggers iḥbāṭ in §14: the cancellation of merit attaches only to the repudiating apostate, not the lapsing-but-believing sinner. The carve-out at the end ("except what the text specifies as capital — gilluy ʿarayot, Sabbath-profanation") preserves the explicit Torah death-penalties as a separate category.
§15b — Resuming "our colleague": the otherworldly death must be shown from the prophets — Isaiah's "their worm shall not die"

(15.) We return to the remainder of the report of the statement of him whose statement on reward and punishment we have been reporting. He said: and we need to describe the otherworldly death (al-mawt al-akhīr) and indicate it from the sayings of the prophets, just as we indicated the otherworldly life. So we say that יְשַׁעְיָהוּ (peace be upon him) said [Isa 66:24] וְיָצְאוּ וְרָאוּ בְּפִגְרֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים הַפֹּשְׁעִים בִּי ("and they shall go forth and look upon the corpses of the men who rebelled against Me") and its completion. So he informed that the people of obedience see the bodies of the people of punishment, the malefactors; and by his mentioning that, we knew that he intended the prostrate ones (al-ṣarʿā) who have no rising — and they are the dead. And his saying [Isa 66:24] תּוֹלַעְתָּם לֹא תָמוּת ("their worm shall not die") distinguished between them and those who died a natural death in which there is no sensation — and [indicated] that there returns to them that whereby they sense the pains by its like; for otherwise, dead bodies — their worm perishes when [the worm] consumes that body by eating it. So [the fact] that the worm persists and does not die means the persistence of the body; and the body persists only by something that sustains it — and that is among the conditions of sensation. So inevitably that body has that whereby it finds the pains, even though [those bodies are] upon their fallen-places (maṣāriʿihā).

: The doubled section-number "15" in Nemoy's text (here §15b) marks the resumption of "our colleague's" abridged treatise after Q's interpolated §§13-15a on iḥbāṭ. The otherworldly death/punishment is now established from the prophets, beginning with Isa 66:24 — the eschatological coda to the very chapter Bab 6 closed on. Q reads "their worm shall not die" / "their fire shall not be quenched" not as a description of ordinary decomposing corpses (whose worms die once the body is consumed) but as a sign that the punished bodies persist, sustained so as to feel pain — i.e., a sensate, embodied otherworldly punishment. The argument from the conditions of sensation (sharāʾiṭ al-ḥiss: a persisting body, capable of feeling) is a kalāmī physical-theory move pressed into eschatology.
§16 — The fire of Tophet, and Daniel's "many who sleep shall awake": the two eternal lots

And the like of that is His saying [Isa 66:24] וְאִשָּׁם לֹא תִכְבֶּה ("and their fire shall not be quenched") — because [ordinary] fires perish and are extinguished and persist only by the persistence of the materials [feeding them]; and only those possessed of sensation [can] be pained and hurt. So this is what he informed of, concerning the meaning of the otherworldly death.

(16.) And the like of that is His saying in another place [Isa 30:33, with Eccl 10:20 conflated in the citation] כִּי עָרוּךְ מֵאֶתְמוּל תָּפְתֶּה גַּם הוּא לַמֶּלֶךְ הֻכָן הֶעְמִיק הִרְחִב מְדֻרָתָהּ אֵשׁ וְעֵצִים הַרְבֵּה נִשְׁמַת יְיָ כְּנַחַל גָּפְרִית בֹּעֲרָה בָּהּ ("for Tophet is ordained of old … deep and wide is its pyre, fire and much wood; the breath of the Lord, like a stream of brimstone, kindles it"). And this is an explicit statement of the otherworldly punishment by fire, and that Gehenna (al-jaḥīm), [the place] of fire and brimstone, is the dwelling of its people. And דָּנִיֵּאל (peace be upon him) said [Dan 12:2] וְרַבִּים מִיְּשֵׁנֵי אַדְמַת עָפָר יָקִיצוּ אֵלֶּה לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם וְאֵלֶּה לַחֲרָפוֹת וּלְדִרְאוֹן עוֹלָם ("and many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, these to eternal life and these to reproaches and to eternal abhorrence"). So he informed that the two classes together — those of the everlasting life and those of the everlasting infamy (al-nakāl) — awake; then he divided them into two divisions, the one for the eternal life and the other for the eternal disgrace and infamy. And this division is the division of death of which the Torah informed, and its meaning became the meaning of punishment; and the other division is the division of life of which the Torah informed.

And a people of those of our religion have denied the resurrection of the dead (iḥyāʾ al-amwāt) and adduced for that proofs from Scripture; we shall mention that and refute their statement on it hereafter. Then he said after that [Dan 12:3] וְהַמַּשְׂכִּלִים יַזְהִרוּ כְּזֹהַר הָרָקִיעַ וּמַצְדִּיקֵי הָרַבִּים [כַּכּוֹכָבִים] ("and the wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who turn many to righteousness [like the stars]"). And this second statement is proper to the righteous, those of the eternal life and the eternal reward, the dwellers of the Garden, who are the rational, rightly-guided ones (al-ʿuqalāʾ al-murshidūn) who chose the obedience that made obligatory for them the eternal life and the eternal reward — as the Torah said [Deut 30:19] וּבָחַרְתָּ בַּחַיִּים לְמַעַן תִּחְיֶה אַתָּה וְזַרְעֶךָ ("and you shall choose life, that you may live, you and your seed").

: The otherworldly punishment by fire: Isa 30:33's Tophet (its "pyre," medurah, kindled by a brimstone stream) is read as the literal Gehenna (al-jaḥīm) of fire and brimstone. Then the climactic prooftext: Dan 12:2, the clearest biblical resurrection text, with its explicit two eternal lots — "eternal life" vs. "eternal abhorrence" — which Q maps directly onto the Torah's life/death = reward/punishment. Note the source's citation conflates Eccl 10:20 (ʿof ha-shamayim yolikh) into the Isa 30:33 lemma — an OCR/marginal-pointer artifact, flagged. Q also flags, for later refutation, the resurrection-deniers "of our religion" (Karaites or Jews who rejected bodily iḥyāʾ al-amwāt) — the promised rebuttal is the "branches" material announced in §24.
§17 — "To a thousand generations" (Exod 20:6; Deut 7:9) means the whole age of the world

(17.) And this is another sort of what is in the Torah of the mention of reward and punishment. God (majestic and exalted) said in [Exod 20:3] לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים עַל פָּנָי ("you shall have no other gods before Me") and said at its end [Exod 20:6] וְעֹשֶׂה חֶסֶד לַאֲלָפִים ("and showing kindness to thousands"), and said in another place [Exod 34:7] וְנַקֵּה לֹא יְנַקֶּה ("[yet] He will by no means clear the guilty") [and] in [Lev 19:18] … and said in it [Exod 20:6] לַאֲלָפִים ("to thousands"). So His saying, in these two places, that He is the doer of kindness to a thousand generations — He did not make its meaning plain in these two places; rather it became plain from another place, namely His saying [Deut 7:9] וְיָדַעְתָּ כִּי יְיָ אֱלֹהֶיךָ הוּא הָאֱלֹהִים הָאֵל הַנֶּאֱמָן שֹׁמֵר הַבְּרִית וְהַחֶסֶד לְאֹהֲבָיו וּלְשֹׁמְרֵי מִצְוֹתָיו לְאֶלֶף דּוֹר ("and you shall know that the Lord your God, He is God, the faithful God who keeps the covenant and the kindness with those who love Him and keep His commandments, to a thousand generations").

So it became plain from His saying here that His saying there, in the place where He said "to a thousand [generations]," is that He meant a thousand centuries (alf qarn). And it is not possible for this thousand-centuries to be [reckoned] for every person who did good and was righteous — for if the thousand were counted from every righteous one, that would entail that the time of the world be without end: for there would be kept for Adam (peace be upon him) a thousand centuries, and for his son a thousand centuries, and for his son's son a thousand centuries, and likewise for every one of the offspring of the pious, and the offspring of the offspring, a thousand centuries; and if at the end of every thousand there is a single righteous one for whom it is kept a thousand centuries, this becomes without end — and this is absurd. And since that is so, it is established that the thousand centuries mentioned in the Torah is not centuries [reckoned] for every single righteous and pious one, nor for his offspring and progeny. Then we found דָּוִד (peace be upon him) saying [Ps 105:8] זָכַר לְעוֹלָם בְּרִיתוֹ דָּבָר צִוָּה לְאֶלֶף דּוֹר ("He has remembered His covenant forever, the word He commanded to a thousand generations") — so he informed that God's ordinances and His command are binding to a thousand generations. So we knew from that, and from what is in the Torah, that this thousand centuries mentioned is the measure of the world and its span, and the time of God's ordinances and His commandments; and that the world is the time of a thousand centuries.

: A second, independent line of argument. The Decalogue's "kindness to thousands [of generations]" (Exod 20:6), clarified by Deut 7:9's "to a thousand generations" (le-elef dor), is taken to mean a thousand qarn (centuries/generations). Q's reductio: if the "thousand" were credited afresh to each righteous individual and his descendants, the world would have to last infinitely — absurd. Therefore "a thousand generations" denotes a fixed total — the entire duration of the world (confirmed by Ps 105:8, where the covenant-command holds "to a thousand generations"). This sets up §§18-19: since God "keeps" the righteous person's merit for the whole age of the world, and no one lives that long, the reward must be paid in another abode — the otherworldly one. (alf qarn = "a thousand centuries/generations"; Q glosses dor as qarn.)
§18 — The length of a "century" computed: the world's span is seventy thousand years

(18.) As for how great the measure of a "century" (qarn) is in years — it must be seventy years, when the centuries of the world are multiplied one by another. And that is [reckoned] from the creation of Adam to the destruction of the [First] Temple and the exile of the nation, [a span] resembling fifty centuries; and the sum of the years [is] some three thousand three hundred and sixty-odd, approximately — so each century comes to resemble seventy years. So it follows from that that the sum of the time of the world is seventy thousand years. So it is established for us that the meaning of that is: that God (holy be His names) keeps, for every righteous and pious one, his righteousness and his piety and his beneficence …

: The arithmetic of the world-age. Q computes the length of a "century"/generation (qarn) empirically: ~50 such qarns spanned Adam to the First Temple's destruction = ~3,360 years, so one qarn ≈ 70 years; hence the "thousand generations" of the world = 70,000 years total. (The figure is offered "approximately," ʿalā al-taqrīb.) The point is not chronological precision but the conclusion that the divine "keeping" of merit is co-extensive with the whole world-age — which no individual can outlive, forcing the reward into the next world (§19). The sentence runs over the page-break into §19.
§19 — Since no one lives a thousand centuries, the reward must be otherworldly

… and what he upheld of God's covenant — which is the Torah, since He informed us that it is the covenant, as He says [Deut 5:2-3] יְיָ אֱלֹהֵינוּ כָּרַת עִמָּנוּ בְּרִית בְּחֹרֵב לֹא אֶת אֲבֹתֵינוּ כָּרַת יְיָ אֶת הַבְּרִית הַזֹּאת ("the Lord our God made a covenant with us at Horeb; not with our fathers did the Lord make this covenant") and its completion. So the righteousness of every possessor of righteousness came to be kept for him until the elapsing of the time of this world and the arrival of the time of the world-to-come — which is after a thousand centuries from the beginning of the time of this world, and that is its [the world's] lifespan; no other [reading] is admissible in the interpretation. And this speaks of the otherworldly reward and gives the lie to the statement of whoever claimed that the Torah did not hold out incentive to otherworldly reward; and it is exceedingly plain.

(19.) And since God (majestic and mighty) safeguarded (ḥaraza) for every righteous one his good and his beneficence and his righteousness until the thousand is completed, and since it is not possible that anyone of mankind live the measure of a thousand centuries, it follows that the reward of every recompensed one is not worldly — since each is cut off (yukhtaram) before the thousand centuries. So it is established that the reward of the righteous is in another abode than this abode, which is the abode of death; for otherwise, what is the thing that is safeguarded for the righteous to a thousand centuries while they are dead?

As for the meaning of His saying [Exod 20:5] פֹּקֵד עֲוֹן אָבוֹת עַל בָּנִים ("visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children") and its completion — we shall expound it in another place than this, that being in the discussion on the Ten Commandments (al-ʿashr kalimāt), since our aim here is only the establishment of reward and punishment from Scripture. And perhaps we shall there also speak on the worldly promise and threat (al-waʿd wa-l-waʿīd al-dunyawiyyayn) mentioned in the Torah, and inform of their cause, and [show] that individuals among the people were not intended by them, and that this enters into the meaning of His saying פֹּקֵד עֲוֹן אָבוֹת עַל בָּנִים — which also refers to the dynasties, kingdoms, and communities (al-duwal wa-l-mamālik wa-l-jamāʿāt), since Scripture does not contradict [itself]. For He said, concerning the individual [Deut 24:16] מִבִּנְיָנָהּ לֹא יוּמְתוּ אָבוֹת עַל בָּנִים ("fathers shall not be put to death for children") …

: The conclusion of the "thousand generations" argument: God safeguards (ḥaraza) the righteous person's merit for the whole age of the world; but no one lives a thousand centuries, and each "is cut off" (yukhtaram) before then — therefore the reward is paid in another abode (the otherworldly one), not in this "abode of death." Q then forestalls the obvious objection (the Decalogue's "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children," Exod 20:5, sounds like worldly corporate recompense) by deferring it to his treatment of "the Ten Commandments" and resolving it through the principle that waʿd/waʿīd dunyawī (worldly promise/threat) target collectives — dynasties and communities — not individuals (Deut 24:16's "fathers shall not die for sons" guaranteeing individual non-transfer of guilt). "Scripture does not contradict itself" (al-kitāb lā yatanāqaḍ) is the governing axiom, as in Bab 6 §10. The cross-reference is to a later (lost or separate) treatment of the Decalogue.
§20 — Ezekiel confirms individual desert; transition to the second class of reward

… and its completion. And יְחֶזְקֵאל also interpreted that by his saying [Ezek 18:20] הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַחֹטֵאת הִיא תָמוּת בֵּן לֹא יִשָּׂא בַּעֲוֹן הָאָב ("the soul that sins, it shall die; a son shall not bear the iniquity of the father") etc. And this [refers] inevitably to individuals and persons — and that whoever commits a sin that does not pass beyond him [to others], none reaps its fruit save he, in himself.

(20.) So since we have mentioned the reward and the recompense that comes to be in the Garden, let us now mention another class of the reward of which the books of revelation (kutub al-tanzīl) spoke — and it is the angelic, spiritual reward (al-thawāb al-malakī al-rūḥānī), which is other than the corporeal [reward] that is in the Garden. For [Scripture] had informed of the passing-away of the heavens and the earth — so where, then, is the Garden and its dwellers, since it has been established that the Garden is upon the earth? And it cannot be that the reward should be cut off (munqaṭiʿan), it being God's recompense in the world that has no cutting-off; and we have also said that the reward of God (exalted) must be complete (tāmm), and that what falls short of eternalization (al-taʾbīd) is not complete — so it follows from that that God's reward is eternalized (muʾabbad). And we shall also mention what indicates its eternalization, from reason and Scripture together.

: A pivot to the second, higher class of reward. The corporeal reward of the Garden faces a problem: Scripture says heaven and earth pass away — but the Garden is on the earth; so the embodied Garden-reward cannot be the final state (reward cannot be "cut off," munqaṭiʿ, and must be muʾabbad, eternalized — the taʾbīd doctrine, glossary §VI). Hence there must be a second reward: the "angelic, spiritual reward" (al-thawāb al-malakī al-rūḥānī), enjoyed by disembodied souls after the cosmos dissolves. This two-stage eschatology (embodied Garden → disembodied angelic state in al-dahr) is the distinctive doctrine of the bab, developed in §§21-23.
§21 — Moses' request to see God's glory: the heavenly host, and the spirit-substances that outlast the world

(21.) We return to the establishing of the angelic, spiritual reward. Of that is the saying of Moses (peace be upon him) to God (mighty and exalted) [Exod 33:18] הַרְאֵנִי נָא אֶת כְּבֹדֶךָ ("show me, I pray, Your glory"); so He answered him by His saying [Exod 33:19] אֲנִי אַעֲבִיר כָּל טוּבִי עַל פָּנֶיךָ ("I will make all My goodness pass before you") and its completion, and His saying [Exod 33:19] וְחַנֹּתִי אֶת אֲשֶׁר אָחֹן ("and I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious") and its completion. So His saying, in the reply — "and My being-gracious to whom I am gracious, and My mercy to whom I show mercy" — it is known from it that [Moses] asked Him to show him His reward together with His majesty. And He said [Exod 33:20] לֹא תוּכַל לִרְאֹת אֶת פָּנָי ("you cannot see My face"), and His saying [Exod 33:22] וְהָיָה בַּעֲבֹר כְּבֹדִי ("and when My glory passes by") and its completion וַהֲסִרֹתִי אֶת כַּפִּי ("and I will remove My hand") and its completion. So it became plain from this statement that He intended the heavenly procession (al-mawkib al-samāwī) and the heavenly majesty; and by His saying וְחַנֹּתִי אֶת אֲשֶׁר אָחֹן ("and My mercy"), it is known that the true goods and the true mercy are only by means of the angels and the heavenly host (al-ʿaskar al-samāwī).

And by that the [appearance of] contradiction was removed — [the contradiction] in Scripture's informing of the passing-away of the world and its perishing and the non-being of the Garden and its people. Then the prophets interpreted that: David (peace be upon him) said [Ps 102:26-29] לְפָנִים הָאָרֶץ יָסַדְתָּ וּמַעֲשֵׂה יָדֶיךָ שָׁמָיִם הֵמָּה יֹאבֵדוּ וְאַתָּה תַעֲמֹד ("of old You founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands; they shall perish, but You shall stand") etc. וְאַתָּה הוּא וּשְׁנוֹתֶיךָ לֹא יִתָּמּוּ בְּנֵי עֲבָדֶיךָ יִשְׁכּוֹנוּ ("but You are He, and Your years shall have no end; the children of Your servants shall dwell [secure]") etc. So he made obligatory, after the passing-away of the world and its perishing, a persistence and a permanence for the Lord of the worlds (majestic and exalted) and for His righteous servants before Him. And it is among the absurd [to suppose] that, with the perishing of the bodies and of place and of time, the righteous remain with God while they are bodies — since the bodies are non-existent [then]; so they are then, of necessity, angelic spirits (arwāḥ malakiyya). And He said [Isa 51:6] …

: The textual basis of the spiritual reward. Moses' request "show me Your glory" (Exod 33:18) and the reply (the "goodness" passing by, the heavenly mawkib and ʿaskar samāwī — procession and host) are read as a glimpse of the angelic reward. The apparent contradiction — Scripture both promises an earthly Garden-reward and foretells the cosmos's dissolution — is resolved by David (Ps 102:26-29): when heaven and earth "perish," God endures and "the children of His servants shall dwell" — necessarily as disembodied "angelic spirits" (arwāḥ malakiyya), since bodies, place, and time are then non-existent. The reasoning is again kalāmī-cosmological (time and place are functions of bodies; when bodies cease, so do they — see §22). The Isa 51:6 lemma opens at the page-foot and continues in §22's run.
§22 — al-dahr vs. time; Zechariah's vision of Joshua the High Priest; the souls' two fates

[Isa 51:6] שְׂאוּ לַשָּׁמַיִם עֵינֵיכֶם … וִישׁוּעָתִי לְעוֹלָם תִּהְיֶה ("lift up your eyes to the heavens … but My salvation shall be forever"). So he informed, too, that after the heavens and the earth dissolve and their people and dwellers die, the deliverance and the discrimination (al-faraj wa-l-furqān) remain for those who deserve them, forever, and the justice of God (majestic and mighty) [endures] century after century. So every eternity conjoined to the world is inevitably temporal — I mean [lasting] to the end of [worldly] time; and every eternity after the world is inevitably perpetual (dahriyya), not temporal — since time has ceased with the ceasing of the bodies, for its cause is only the celestial motions: so when there is no mover, there are no moved things, and the effects of the motions are not. As for al-dahr (perpetual duration), it is but a single everlasting power (quwwa wāḥida sarmadiyya) that the motions do not annihilate and the distances do not interrupt, since these are non-existent. And were there no further states after the world, He would not have said, after the perishing of the world, "My discrimination and My deliverance shall be forever" — since [then] there would be no existents whom the discrimination and the deliverance of the Maker (mighty and exalted) reach; and likewise His saying "and My justice, which is century after century." So it is not a statement that ought to let any ambiguity enter upon those of discernment and pure intellects, by their saying that the successive centuries and births have ceased and procreation has come to an end — for this statement falls only upon the past centuries; for the people of reward, who are the people of the first centuries, and whoever deserved God's discrimination (His praises be exalted), have an ordering in their creation that was, and in their being-newly-fashioned (ibdāʿ) that is promised to them; so they are inevitably successive centuries [gathered together]. So [the statement] indicated by this that they were not the people of a single abode, but rather the peoples of many abodes, whom [God] gathered — on the precedence of some over others, and the succeeding of some upon others — to the abode of the world-to-come, so that they came to be in it together.

(22.) And likewise is what Zechariah the prophet (peace be upon him) recounted of the story of יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן יְהוֹצָדָק הַכֹּהֵן — that he saw, in prophecy, as it were the angel called the Plotter, the Adversary (al-mukayyid al-muʿānid), standing at his right to oppose him and plot against him; and that upon [Joshua] were filthy garments (thiyāb filādha), for which reason the Plotter wished to plot against him; so God said to the Plotter [Zech 3:2] יִגְעַר יְיָ בְּךָ הַשָּׂטָן ("the Lord rebuke you, O Adversary!"). And יְהוֹשֻׁעַ (peace be upon him) was a priest (kohen) in the house of the Merciful, and was of the pious among the [people] — except that upon him were those stains that appeared in [contrast to] the purity of his garments; and God said to the angels standing before Him [Zech 3:4] הָסִירוּ הַבְּגָדִים הַצּוֹאִים מֵעָלָיו ("remove the filthy garments from upon him") and its completion, and said to him: I have removed from you your sins and delivered you from your stains. Then He said to him [Zech 3:7] אִם בִּדְרָכַי תֵּלֵךְ וְאִם אֶת מִשְׁמַרְתִּי תִשְׁמֹר ("if you walk in My ways and keep My charge") etc., [and:] "and I will set for you passages among these standing ones" — meaning by them the angels. So what statement is sounder concerning the angelic reward and the becoming of the pious and the righteous, after the perishing of the world and their separation from their bodies and their persistence as bare spirits, [proceeding] to the angels and the joining of the heavenly hosts? And this is a view that the Hebrews used to hold, transmitting it [one from another] and agreeing upon it; and it was for them in the place of primary cognition (al-maʿrifa al-ūlā) — [namely] the persistence of the spirits after the separation from the bodies.

What indicates that, too, is the saying of אֲבִיגַיִל to David [1 Sam 25:29] וְהָיְתָה נֶפֶשׁ אֲדֹנִי צְרוּרָה בִּצְרוֹר הַחַיִּים אֵת יְיָ אֱלֹהֶיךָ ("and the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life with the Lord your God"). For she met him only with what was established with her and with all the people of the religion (ahl al-milla), according to what they inherited [as tradition]. And in that is an indication that the souls are persisting substances (jawāhir bāqiya): of them is what is in the "binding of life" (ṣirār al-ḥayāh) on high and in the heavens, with God — or with God (mighty and exalted); and of them is what is roving, perpetually in motion, that neither settles nor rests. And this is the way of everything flung with the cup of the sling: so it indicated that the souls of the wicked and the evil come to be in the station of the roving things that move with motions of compulsion, driving, and constraint, just as the sling drives whatever is set in it. So this life, in which is the "binding" of the souls of the pious, cannot be one that goes back to the life of this world, since He said of it "with God" — or "with God (mighty and exalted)"; and this inevitably indicates that it is an eternal, divine life (ḥayāh abadiyya ilāhiyya).

: The metaphysics of al-dahr (perpetual duration) and the climactic prooftexts. Q distinguishes zamān (time — a function of celestial motion, which ceases when bodies cease) from al-dahr (a single everlasting, motionless "power," quwwa wāḥida sarmadiyya) — so the post-cosmic reward is dahrī (perpetual), not temporal. Three prooftexts ground the disembodied soul-state: Isa 51:6 ("My salvation forever" — outlasting the dissolved cosmos); Zech 3:1-7 (Joshua the High Priest cleansed before the Satan/Adversary, given "passages among the standing ones" = the angels — read as the righteous soul joining the angelic host); and 1 Sam 25:29 (Abigail's "bundle of life," ṣeror ha-ḥayyim) — the righteous soul "bound" with God, the wicked soul "slung" away (the sling-stone image from the same verse's continuation). The "primary cognition" (al-maʿrifa al-ūlā) claim — that the soul's survival was a received, consensus Hebrew belief — grounds the doctrine in tradition as well as reason.
