§23 — The two otherworldly recompenses summarized; the soul between death and resurrection

(23.) So it is now established that the recompense of individuals among mankind is of two kinds, both of them otherworldly. The one comes to be after the restoration of the spirits to the bodies, in the Garden and in Gehenna, as we have made plain — until the world reaches the end of the time appointed for it, and the rest of the bodies, and place and time (which are conjoined to the bodies), pass away. And the second comes to be at the persistence of the spirits belonging to those bodies, in the al-dahr (perpetual duration) that the motions do not interrupt nor annihilate — rather it is a single everlasting power — and [it is] the joining of its righteous ones to the ranks of the angels, and their entry into their company, and their being in the heavenly host, and the supreme felicity by their nearness to their Maker (majestic and mighty); and the becoming of the wicked spirits, which have departed the corporeal punishment, to the spiritual punishment, which is the opposite of that in which are the spirits of the righteous.

So if a questioner asks about the spirits, after their separation from the bodies by death, until they are raised a second time in their bodies — where is their place? — [then we say] that what is admissible in our view is that they are in the spiritual recompense, since it does not occur to the intellects that they remain neglected, not [enjoying or suffering] the fruits of their deeds and their deserts (istiḥqāqāt). Except that the pleasure in which the soul of the obedient one is, after its separation from the body until the time it is raised, does not match the pleasure of the bliss of the world-to-come [proper], but is rather below it — though of its kind; and it comes to that supreme reward only after the reward of the Garden is converted (yanqalib) to that [final] recompense. And likewise is the statement concerning the disobediences [and their punishment]. And some of our colleagues have, on that, a statement which we defer to the twenty-first bab; and a people refused that this should be so, and clung to things from Scripture — so we defer their statement on that, in the refutation of them, to hereafter.

: The systematic summary of the two-stage otherworldly recompense — (1) embodied, in the Garden/Gehenna, until the cosmos dissolves; (2) disembodied-angelic, in al-dahr, thereafter — and the resolution of the "intermediate state" question: between individual death and the general resurrection, the soul already experiences a lesser foretaste of its desert (istiḥqāq), "of the same kind" as but "below" the final bliss, until the Garden-reward is "converted" into the final dahrī reward. Q twice defers contested points: a fuller treatment by "some of our colleagues" to Bab 21 (his anti-Qūmisī defense of naẓar, per glossary §III), and the rebuttal of the resurrection-deniers (flagged in §16) to the "branches" announced in §24.
§24 — Conclusion: the positive case is complete; transition to the rebuttal of objectors

(24.) We have [now] accomplished what we intended of the abridgment of what some of our colleagues said on the establishment of reward and punishment from the Torah and from the books of the prophets; and we ourselves have also added [material] in support and exposition of that — [material] that refutes the statement of whoever claims that the Torah holds out incentive only to the worldly goods, and gives warning only against its evils and its hardships, and that it contained no otherworldly reward and no punishment. And in order that … there have been mentioned of that many parallels, [some of] which I have left off mentioning out of dislike of prolixity in this place, and because in some of what we have mentioned of that there is sufficiency. So since we have mentioned that, we need to mention what is in it of the branches (al-furūʿ), together with the statement of whoever differed from us in some of what we have set forth, and the refutation of them — so that the discussion of that may be complete and exhaustive; and with God is the strength. Let us begin of that with the refutation of whoever invalidated the life of the dead (ḥayāt al-amwāt, the resurrection).

And a people of our colleagues have claimed that the Torah's expansiveness in mentioning the worldly recompense, rather than the recompense of the world-to-come, is because the otherworldly reward is known by reason (maʿlūm ʿaqlan), needing no proof and no demonstration — since it is impossible for the Sage (al-ḥakīm) to command and to forbid yet not reward the one who obeys nor punish the one who disobeys; for we [plainly] see the disobedient sometimes blessed in this world, and the obedient sometimes tried with afflictions and calamities; and since that is so, and the Maker is just, it is established that there is here a reward in [some abode] other than this abode. They said: His expansiveness in [mentioning] the worldly recompense is only for two reasons. One of them is the inclination of souls to the hastening of the boon and their dislike of the deferral of the hateful [thing]; and the second is the establishing of the proof and the argument for the prophets, when what they promised and informed of comes to pass. And it suffices you of that [to consider] a single promise — namely His saying [2 Kgs 19:29 / Isa 37:30, in the Sennacherib oracle] בְּשִׁשִּׁים וְשֶׁבַע [שָׁנָה] וְלֹא יַעֲמֹד אִישׁ אֶת אַרְצֶךָ ("[within] sixty and seven [years] no man shall stand against your land"), and the completion of that — three hundred years — and their witnessing it throughout the length of their stay in the land. And they adduced, as proof of the obligatoriness of the latter reward, the patience (ṣabr) of the saints (al-awliyāʾ) under the trials of the world, and their giving of their souls to destruction in obedience to the Maker (mighty and exalted) — like the patience of Abraham in the slaughtering of the [child of his] heart's-blood, and likewise the self-giving of חֲנַנְיָה, and like the patience of דָּנִיֵּאל under what used to befall him from the nation in obedience to the Creator (mighty and exalted), and likewise the patience of a company of the prophets under killing from [their enemies], and like the self-giving of חֲנַנְיָה מִישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָה to the burning, and דָּנִיֵּאל to the lions — and the like of that is much. For had they not been certain of the reward, they would not have done it.

: The bab's conclusion and bridge. §24 closes the positive case (Q's abridgment-plus-supplement of his Karaite predecessor's eschatology) and announces the turn to "the branches" (al-furūʿ) — the dialectical rebuttal of objectors, beginning with the deniers of bodily resurrection (ḥayāt al-amwāt). It then records a further Karaite view (held by "a people of our colleagues"): the Torah dwells on worldly recompense not because there is no otherworldly one — that is known by reason (since a just Sage must requite obedience and disobedience, yet worldly fortune visibly fails to track desert) — but for two pedagogical reasons: souls crave immediate reward and dread deferred punishment; and fulfilled worldly prophecies (e.g. the Sennacherib oracle, 2 Kgs 19:29 / Isa 37:30) furnish demonstrable proof of the prophets' veracity. The catalogue of martyr-exemplars (Abraham's near-sacrifice of Isaac; Daniel and the three youths Hananiah/Mishael/Azariah braving the furnace and the lions) clinches it: their willingness to die in obedience presupposes certainty of [otherworldly] reward. - An abridged source, with Q's interpolations. The bab is, by Q's own framing, a digest of a lost treatise by "one of our colleagues" (an unnamed earlier Karaite), interleaved with Q's own additions. The seams are visible: "he said" (qāla) introduces the source (§§1, 15b, 23, 24); "we say" / "we need" (naqūlu / naḥtāju) introduces Q's voice and his interpolated discussions (notably the iḥbāṭ excursus of §§13-15a, anchored on Num 15:30's be-yad ramah). Nemoy's doubled section-number "15" (§15a / §15b) marks precisely the point where Q's interpolation ends and the source resumes. The bab is thus a rare window onto a pre-Qirqisānī Karaite eschatology that Q both transmits and corrects.

- The governing lexical thesis: ḥayāh/mawt = thawāb/ʿiqāb. The structural spine of §§3-12 is the claim that, in the Hebrew tongue, "life" and "death" carry the technical force of otherworldly reward and punishment. The proof is cumulative and almost entirely philological: the Eden "death" that is not same-day death but exile from the abode of life (§3); the two goods of Deut 6:24-25, "all the days" (worldly) vs. "to keep us alive as this day" (otherworldly) (§5); Qohelet's demonstration that worldly fortune does not track desert (§9); and — the master-stroke — Ezekiel's second death (Ezek 18:26), which cannot be a literal death since "the dead man cannot die after his death," and so must be otherworldly punishment (§10). 2 Sam 12:13 ("you shall not die," to a David who did die) and Deut 33:6 ("let Reuben live") seal the equation (§11).

- A two-stage, body-and-soul eschatology. Q's predecessor (and Q) hold a distinctive bicompartmental doctrine: (1) a first, embodied recompense in the Garden / Gehenna on the earth, following the resurrection (iʿāda) of body-and-soul together (Eccl 12:7 for the soul's survival; Ps 104:29-30 for re-embodiment; Dan 12:2 for the two lots) — §§7, 16; and (2) a second, disembodied angelic, spiritual recompense in al-dahr (perpetual duration), after the cosmos itself dissolves (Ps 102:26-29; Isa 51:6; Zech 3; 1 Sam 25:29's "bundle of life") — §§20-23. The transition between the two is the dissolution of bodies, place, and time. An intermediate state between individual death and the general resurrection is posited as a lesser foretaste of the soul's desert (§23).

- The "thousand generations" argument (§§17-19). An independent line, not lexical but quasi-arithmetical: the Decalogue's ḥesed la-alafim / Deut 7:9's le-elef dor is read as "a thousand centuries" = the whole age of the world (computed at ~70,000 years from a ~70-year qarn, §18). Since God "safeguards" the righteous one's merit for that whole span, and no one lives so long, the reward must be paid in another abode. The argument turns on the premise that "a thousand generations" cannot be reckoned afresh per individual without entailing an infinite world (the reductio of §17).

- The metaphysics of al-dahr. §22 supplies the bab's one genuinely technical metaphysical move: the distinction between zamān (time — an effect of celestial motion, hence non-existent once bodies cease) and al-dahr (a single everlasting, motionless "power," quwwa sarmadiyya). This underwrites the claim that the second reward is dahrī (perpetual), not merely zamānī (temporal/finite) — i.e., genuinely eternal (muʾabbad), satisfying the kalāmī requirement that divine recompense be tāmm (complete) and therefore not "cut off" (§§6, 20).

- The iḥbāṭ / takfīr excursus (§§13-15a). Q's interpolated treatment of the cancellation of works is squarely Bahshamī. The reversibility of destiny (Ezek 18: prior merit erased by apostasy, prior sin by repentance) generates the "hundred-years problem"; Q's answer (with "some of the people of inquiry") is that cancellation is not unconditional — Prov 24:16 is qualified, and iḥbāṭ attaches only where the lapse is joined to takdhīb (repudiation) and nadam (regret), i.e., the be-yad ramah disposition of Num 15:30 (defiant contempt, "despising the word of the Lord"), not to a mere lapse by one who still believes. This preserves al-ʿadl (divine justice) by distinguishing the contemptuous apostate from the weak-but-believing sinner.

- Cross-references to other works. Q defers, as elsewhere in the Maqala, several matters to other treatments: the poqed ʿavon / corporate-vs-individual recompense problem to "the discussion on the Ten Commandments" (§19); a contested point on the intermediate-state recompense to Bab 21 (his defense of naẓar, per glossary §III); and the refutation of the resurrection-deniers to the forthcoming "branches" (§§16, 24). These confirm the Anwār's design as a cross-referencing whole.

- The polemical frame. Though the bab's content is constructive eschatology, its polemical target is explicit at both ends: it answers the Christian charge (set up at the close of Bab 6) that the Torah contains no doctrine of eternal otherworldly reward and punishment (§1), and it repeatedly rebuts "whoever claims that the Torah held out incentive only to worldly goods" (§§9, 19, 24) — a charge leveled by Christian supersessionists and, in a different key, presupposed by the modern Wellhausenian reading. Q's response is that the otherworldly doctrine is present in the Torah by limit-case statement (the §2 qiyās principle) and drawn out explicitly by the later prophets.
